# What I Learned Building a Thermal-Chemical EOR Experiment for Niger Delta Heavy Oil

**Paul Madu — July 2026**

---

Most software developers have never held a core sample. Most petroleum engineers have never deployed to production. I spent my final year of university sitting uncomfortably in the middle of both worlds, and I want to write about what that taught me — because I think it is the most honest thing I can put on this portfolio.

---

## Why Heavy Oil in the Niger Delta Is a Genuinely Hard Problem

Nigeria produces over two million barrels of oil per day. What most people do not know is that a significant portion of the Niger Delta's remaining reserves are classified as **heavy oil** — crude with an API gravity below 20, meaning it is thick, viscous, and does not flow easily through reservoir rock the way light crude does.

My crude oil samples had an API gravity of **17 to 19**. To put that in context: water has an API of 10, light crude is above 30, and heavy oil sits between 10 and 22. At reservoir temperatures, Niger Delta heavy oil moves through rock the way cold honey moves through a sponge.

The geological conditions make it worse. Niger Delta reservoirs are largely **unconsolidated sands** — the grains are not cemented together the way sandstone is. High clay content. Variable porosity. Our experimental samples were at **20% porosity**, which is reasonable, but the clay minerals swell when they contact fresh water, blocking pore throats and trapping oil that was almost within reach.

Primary recovery methods — natural pressure depletion — typically recover less than 10% of the oil in place from these reservoirs. Waterflooding, the most common secondary method, performs poorly because the viscosity contrast between water and heavy oil causes fingering — the water finds the path of least resistance, bypasses the oil, and you produce mostly water with very little crude.

That leaves Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR). And this is where things get interesting.

---

## What We Actually Did

My final year research was titled **"Enhancing Heavy Oil Recovery in the Niger Delta through Thermal-Chemical Methods: An Experimental Approach."** I worked with a team of five, under the supervision of Engr. J. E. Odo, and we conducted our experiments at the University of Port Harcourt's petroleum engineering laboratory.

We investigated two things simultaneously:

**Thermal EOR** — specifically steam injection. The idea is simple: heat reduces viscosity dramatically. Heavy oil that barely moves at 30°C can flow freely at 200°C. Steam injection is the dominant EOR method for heavy oil globally — California's San Joaquin Valley, Canada's oil sands, Venezuela's Orinoco Belt. But it is expensive, energy intensive, and in Niger Delta conditions, heat losses to the surrounding formation are severe.

**Chemical EOR** — specifically surfactants and polymer flooding. Surfactants reduce interfacial tension between oil and water, allowing the water to mobilise oil it would otherwise bypass. Polymers increase the viscosity of the injected water, improving the sweep efficiency and reducing the fingering problem.

What we wanted to know was: **what happens when you combine them?**

We designed and ran core flooding experiments — injecting fluids through cylindrical rock samples saturated with our Niger Delta crude oil — under controlled temperature and pressure conditions. I developed a novel chemical mixture combining surfactant and polymer agents at concentrations optimised for our crude's specific viscosity and the reservoir's clay mineralogy.

Then we ran two sets of experiments: **steam flooding alone**, and **hot chemical flooding** — steam combined with our chemical mixture — at different temperatures and injection rates.

---

## The Finding That Surprised Us

We expected steam to win at high temperatures. What we found was more useful:

**Hot chemical flooding at 80°C outperformed steam flooding alone** — achieving comparable or higher recovery rates at a significantly lower operating temperature.

80°C is the key number. Steam flooding typically requires injection temperatures of 200°C or higher. The energy required to generate and maintain that steam, the heat losses to surrounding strata, the wellbore heat loss — all of these make high-temperature steam flooding expensive and technically challenging in Niger Delta conditions where reservoir depths and geology make steam delivery inefficient.

Our results suggested that the surfactant-polymer combination was doing something important: it was mobilising oil that the thermal component alone could not reach. The chemical mixture was altering wettability — changing the affinity between the rock surface and the oil — and reducing interfacial tension to the point where displacement efficiency improved significantly even at lower temperatures.

We then used **thermal simulation software** to calibrate our experimental results through history matching, building predictive models of how the combined thermal-chemical approach would perform across a range of injection scenarios, depths, and reservoir conditions beyond what we could test in the laboratory.

The economic analysis was equally important. Lower operating temperature means lower energy cost. Lower injection pressure means less wellbore wear. The combined approach, even accounting for the cost of chemical agents, showed better economics than high-temperature steam alone at the reservoir conditions we modelled.

---

## What We Could Not Do — And Why It Matters

Our undergraduate research had real limitations, and I want to be honest about them because they are the reason I am now pursuing this at postgraduate level.

Our core samples were small — standard laboratory plugs, not field-scale. The pore-scale physics that determines how oil mobilises at the grain-to-grain level was not something we could observe directly. We had no CT scanner, no synchrotron imaging, no micro-CT facility. We were working with bulk recovery measurements, not pore-scale displacement visualisation.

Our simulation model was calibrated to our lab experiments, not to a specific Niger Delta field. History matching to sparse laboratory data has limitations — the predictive model has significant uncertainty bounds that we could not fully quantify with our tools.

And our most important recommendation — the one I keep thinking about — was one we could not execute:

**Develop machine learning proxy models to predict oil flow rates from key reservoir parameters, eliminating the need for extensive experimental analysis.**

The logic is straightforward. Running a full thermal simulation for each combination of temperature, pressure, chemical concentration, injection rate, and reservoir property is computationally expensive. A trained ML model that has learned the relationships from a large simulation dataset can make the same prediction in milliseconds. For an operator trying to optimise an injection strategy across hundreds of wells in a field, that difference matters enormously.

We recommended it. We did not have the data, the tools, or the time to build it.

---

## Why This Sits at the Intersection of Everything I Do

I have been writing software professionally for five years. I build in Python, JavaScript, Next.js, Node.js, PostgreSQL. I built SempaiHQ — a live Web3 platform on Solana mainnet. I have deployed code to production that real users depend on.

And I have an undergraduate degree in petroleum engineering and real experimental data from real Niger Delta crude oil.

The ML proxy model we recommended in our research is a Python problem. It is a Pandas problem, a Scikit-learn problem, a data pipeline problem. It is the exact kind of problem I have been building the skills to solve for five years — I just did not know until my final year that it was also the exact problem the petroleum engineering world needs solved.

The Niger Delta's stranded heavy oil reserves are not stranded because the oil is not there. They are stranded because the tools to recover it cost-effectively have not been built yet at the scale and precision that modern machine learning makes possible.

That is what I am working toward. A postgraduate research project combining the experimental foundation I built at FUTO and UNIPORT, the ML and software engineering skills I have built independently, and the rigorous academic supervision of researchers who have spent careers on exactly this problem.

I am in active conversations with petroleum engineering research groups in Australia and the United States. If you are a researcher, a professor, or an engineer working on EOR optimisation, computational reservoir modelling, or ML for energy — I would genuinely like to hear from you.

---

## Technical Stack (For the Developers Reading This)

The simulation and data analysis work used thermal reservoir simulation software for history matching and a Python-based analytics pipeline I built independently:

- **Python / Pandas / NumPy** — production data processing and decline curve automation
- **Matplotlib / Seaborn** — reservoir performance visualisation
- **Scikit-learn** — the foundation for the ML proxy model work I am now developing
- **Jupyter Notebook** — experimental data analysis and modelling

The next iteration — which is what the postgraduate research would build — would likely involve:

- Neural network proxy models trained on large simulation ensembles
- Gaussian Process regression for uncertainty quantification
- Bayesian optimisation for injection parameter optimisation
- Possibly physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that embed the governing fluid flow equations directly into the model architecture

If any of that sounds interesting to collaborate on, my email is at the bottom of this page.

---

*Paul Madu is a Full-Stack Software Engineer and Petroleum Engineering graduate from the Federal University of Technology Owerri, Nigeria. He built SempaiHQ (sempaihq.com), a live Web3 platform on Solana, and is pursuing postgraduate research in thermal-chemical EOR optimisation using machine learning. Find him at github.com/paulphysio.*
